citation: A committee of five representing the Association of Teachers of Psychology in Iowa. (1911). Preparation for Examinations in Psychology. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.apa.org/pubs/journals/edu
title: Recommended list of ten psychology textbooks with Elementary and Advanced requirements
description: To secure a uniform basis for the examinations, the committee recommends ten texts, including Betts, Angell, Kirkpatrick, James, Seashore, Judd, Dewey, Titchener, Calkins, and Thorndike, each annotated (e.g., Seashore's is "A manual of experiments not requiring any laboratory"). The article states "In the Elementary examination, three of these are required; in the Advanced, six." Special books are Kirkpatrick, Seashore, and Dewey; the others are general introductions. A supplementary reference list for public libraries is also given.
requirements: Candidates select two general and one special text for the Elementary examination, four general and two special for the Advanced
constraints: The state examination will be based specifically upon the recommended books only until January 1, 1915, with a revision published January 1, 1914
target_learners: Teachers seeking Elementary or Advanced psychology certification in Iowa
target_learning_goals: Preparation for uniform state psychology examinations
key_sources: A committee of five representing the Association of Teachers of Psychology in Iowa. (1911). Preparation for Examinations in Psychology. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.apa.org/pubs/journals/edu

citation: Vania Dimitrova. (2003). STyLE-OLM: Interactive Open Learner Modelling. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197312
title: Adaptive learning systems should diagnose learners through interactive open learner modelling
description: Because diagnosing a learner's cognitive capacity is crucial for adaptive systems, the article recommends conceiving diagnosis as an interactive process: systems should let the learner discuss and jointly construct the learner model. The authors argue IOLM "is a fruitful approach which may be employed in intelligent learning environments".
requirements: An intelligent learning environment that opens the learner model to inspection and negotiation with the learner
target_learners: learners using adaptive computer-based learning systems
target_learning_goals: improved diagnosis of the learner's cognitive state
examples: STyLE-OLM implements this approach by having the system and learner discuss and together construct the learner model
key_sources: Vania Dimitrova. (2003). STyLE-OLM: Interactive Open Learner Modelling. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197312

article_title: Characterizing academic performance in pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia with population-based achievement tests.
citation: Al‐Kaylani HM, Reasoner EE, Loeffler BT, Mott SL, Madasu S, Liu A, Langbehn K, Conrad AL, Dickens D, Grafft A, Harshman L, Modi AJ, van der Plas E. (2022). Characterizing academic performance in pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia with population‐based achievement tests. Cancer Reports. https://doi.org/10.1002/cnr2.1560
title: Iowa Assessments obtained in a school setting as an ecologically valid measure of academic performance
description: The Iowa Assessments are validated, annually administered achievement tests measuring reading, math, and science in Iowa public and private schools. The article uses school-administered Iowa Assessment scores precisely because psychological achievement tests lack ecological validity: "these measures are typically administered in a quiet testing space with a dedicated examiner. By contrast, most school activities occur while experiencing significant environmental distractions." The tests show composite reliability coefficients of 0.927–0.983 and strong associations with ACT scores.
requirements: Partnership with an educational agency (the Iowa Department of Education) to obtain statewide test scores and program-participation data
constraints: Per the authors' agreement with the Iowa Department of Education, state means could not be specified on plots
examples: The study collected 269 observations across grades 3–11 from 63 ALL survivors treated between 2000 and 2019 at the University of Iowa
key_sources: Al‐Kaylani HM, Reasoner EE, Loeffler BT, Mott SL, Madasu S, Liu A, Langbehn K, Conrad AL, Dickens D, Grafft A, Harshman L, Modi AJ, van der Plas E. (2022). Characterizing academic performance in pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia with population‐based achievement tests. Cancer Reports. https://doi.org/10.1002/cnr2.1560

article_title: Framework for interprofessional case conferences - empirically sound and competence-oriented communication concept for interprofessional teaching.
citation: Posenau André, Handgraaf Marietta. (2021). Framework for interprofessional case conferences – empirically sound and competence-oriented communication concept for interprofessional teaching. GMS Journal for Medical Education. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2021-38/zma001461.shtml
title: Use a competence-oriented performance examination (iOSCE) driven by the framework rather than outcome-only assessment
description: Because "assessment drives learning", the article argues a competence-oriented examination is needed at module end. The framework makes the process observable and evaluable with an empirical basis instead of evaluator introspection, since each discussed aspect "can be captured empirically". Basing evaluation exclusively on case-conference outcomes is judged unsatisfactory; performance in interprofessional interaction is the most relevant criterion.
requirements: An examination format that captures the process aspects empirically
constraints: Until now teaching concentrated on cases at the expense of communication development
examples: In the 7th semester an interprofessional objective structured clinical examination (iOSCE) is used as the graded module exam
key_sources: Posenau André, Handgraaf Marietta. (2021). Framework for interprofessional case conferences – empirically sound and competence-oriented communication concept for interprofessional teaching. GMS Journal for Medical Education. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2021-38/zma001461.shtml

article_title: Optimization Of Simulations And Activities For A New Introductory Quantum Mechanics Curriculum
citation: Antje Kohnle, Charles Baily, Christopher Hooley and Bruce Torrance. (2013). Optimization of Simulations and Activities for a New Introductory Quantum Mechanics Curriculum. http://quantumphysics.iop.org
title: Institute of Physics New Quantum Curriculum simulations and activities for introductory quantum mechanics starting from two-level systems
description: The New Quantum Curriculum (quantumphysics.iop.org) is a set of "online texts and interactive simulations with accompanying activities for an introductory course in quantum mechanics starting from two-level systems". One author designed 17 interactive simulations and activities covering linear algebra, fundamental quantum mechanics concepts, single photon interference, the Bloch sphere representation, entanglement, local hidden variables and quantum information. The article describes trialing and refining these resources with students.
requirements: Designed to be used as self-contained instructional resources via the two-tab interface
constraints: Observation sessions so far limited to a relatively small number of students from a single institution, and only a small number of simulations tested in courses
target_learners: undergraduate physics majors in an introductory quantum mechanics / modern physics course
examples: The hidden variable simulation was used in computer classroom workshops at St Andrews and in homework at Boulder
key_sources: Antje Kohnle, Charles Baily, Christopher Hooley and Bruce Torrance. (2013). Optimization of Simulations and Activities for a New Introductory Quantum Mechanics Curriculum. https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.1483

article_title: A new introductory quantum mechanics curriculum
citation: Kohnle A, Bozhinova I, Browne D, Everitt M, Fomins A, Kok P, Kulaitis G, Prokopas M, Raine D and Swinbank E. (2013). A new introductory quantum mechanics curriculum. https://quantumphysics.iop.org
title: IOP New Quantum Curriculum: free online learning and teaching materials for introductory quantum mechanics starting from two-level systems
description: The Institute of Physics New Quantum Curriculum consists of "freely available online learning and teaching materials (quantumphysics.iop.org) for a first course in university quantum mechanics starting from two-level systems". The core content is around 80 short articles co-authored by leading experts, arranged in themes, with 17 interactive simulations with accompanying activities and problem sets. Materials can be used flexibly, from supplements to existing courses to a complete programme, and solutions to activities are available to instructors.
requirements: Users are asked to sign up to the resource, which helps with evaluation, monitoring use and building a community of users
constraints: Due to the complexity of the simulations, these are best viewed on larger screens, with some functionality lost on a smartphone
examples: All content is downloadable, articles in pdf format and simulations in shockwave, to encourage use in lectures and as handouts
key_sources: Kohnle A, Bozhinova I, Browne D, Everitt M, Fomins A, Kok P, Kulaitis G, Prokopas M, Raine D and Swinbank E. (2013). A new introductory quantum mechanics curriculum. https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.1484

article_title: Student Variability in Learning Advanced Physics
citation: T. Sampson, and M. Hilke. (2013). Student Variability in Learning Advanced Physics. arXiv:1307.6144v1 [physics.ed-ph]. https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.6144
title: iOLM: an iterative Online Learning Machine that adapts content pace per student in a web-based physics module
description: The iOLM is a php server-side web module that "provides new learning content to each student based on their individual learning pace and tracks their progress individually". The main topic is divided into 5 levels (subtopics), each with 3 sublevels using different learning approaches; quizzes with randomly selected questions gate movement, with the transition algorithm printed as (n,m) → (n+1,m) on success and regressions on failure, until the level-6 posttest. Success was "defined as less than two incorrect answers for each quiz", with a 40-quiz limit. It supplemented a conventional classroom course and counted as online homework.
requirements: Web format for flexibility and web-based database management to monitor each student's progress, with secure cryptography or anonymous IDs for confidentiality
constraints: Some students created fake practice accounts, whose final trajectories had to be discarded; some pretest scores were marked as zeros and repeated submissions occurred, reducing usable data
target_learners: second- or third-year undergraduate physics majors
target_learning_goals: mastering reflection and refraction of electromagnetic waves at expertise level 3, covering five knowledge levels from fields at an interface to reflection on a metal interface
examples: The module ran over a two-week period in course phys 342 at McGill; figure 5 shows all class trajectories colour-coded by pace, and typical fast, average, and stuck paths are shown in figures 2–4
key_sources: T. Sampson, and M. Hilke. (2013). Student Variability in Learning Advanced Physics. arXiv:1307.6144v1 [physics.ed-ph]. https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.6144

article_title: Student Variability in Learning Advanced Physics
citation: T. Sampson, and M. Hilke. (2013). Student Variability in Learning Advanced Physics. arXiv:1307.6144v1 [physics.ed-ph]. https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.6144
title: Granular level-and-sublevel content structure with randomised quizzes and immediate feedback in an adaptive online module
description: The iOLM structures content as five levels of knowledge (derivation of fields at an interface, reflection and Snell's law, angular dependence of TM-wave amplitudes, TE case, metal-interface reflection), each divided into three learning-approach sublevels. "The division in many levels and sublevels also allowed for a more granular feed-back system to the students, which was shown to be the most important factor in computer assisted instructional approaches." After each quiz the student receives the score and the list of correct and wrong questions; retakes re-randomise questions and their order.
requirements: A large data set of questions per level from which quiz questions are randomly selected
constraints: Success requires fewer than two incorrect answers per quiz, with a maximum of 40 quizzes before a student is considered stuck and no posttest data can be collected
target_learning_goals: mastery of each subtopic level before progression, measured by quiz success
examples: Figure 3 shows a typical average trajectory in which the student regressed from level 2 to level 1 before eventually reaching level 6; figure 4 shows a stuck student unable to pass level 4 within the 40-quiz limit
key_sources: T. Sampson, and M. Hilke. (2013). Student Variability in Learning Advanced Physics. arXiv:1307.6144v1 [physics.ed-ph]. https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.6144

article_title: Bilgisayar Muhendisligi Egitiminde Teknoloji Egilimlerinin Takip Edilmesi
citation: Ahmet Murat Türk, Alper Bilge. (2015). Bilgisayar Mühendisliği Eğitiminde Teknoloji Eğilimlerinin Takip Edilmesi / Following Technology Trends in Computer Engineering Education. EJOIR – Aralık 2015 IWCEA Özel Sayısı Cilt 3. https://dergipark.org.tr/en/pub/euroerj
title: Internet of things and wearable technologies as proposed curriculum topics centered on scenario-based system design
description: The article defines the internet of things as the capability of everyday objects to connect to the internet network and send and receive data, covering applications from smart cities and e-health to industrial control. It proposes a course focusing on how system design should be done, since designs are application-specific and need-driven. It illustrates with an electronic-card smart greenhouse automation for areas with limited internet and electricity access (Şekil 1), stating a student needs knowledge of databases, microprocessors, computer networks, mobile application development and web page development, so such a course targets senior students. Wearable technologies are treated as a possible sub-branch of IoT.
requirements: Students need database, microprocessor, computer network, mobile development and web development knowledge before such a course
constraints: The proposed course addresses senior (final-year) students because of its prerequisite breadth
examples: A smart greenhouse automation using mobile connection was proposed for an area with restricted internet and electricity access (Turk, Sora Gunal, & Gurel, 2015)
key_sources: Ahmet Murat Türk, Alper Bilge. (2015). Bilgisayar Mühendisliği Eğitiminde Teknoloji Eğilimlerinin Takip Edilmesi / Following Technology Trends in Computer Engineering Education. EJOIR – Aralık 2015 IWCEA Özel Sayısı Cilt 3. https://dergipark.org.tr/en/pub/euroerj

article_title: The mobile information and educational environment of higher educational institution
citation: Moiseienko N., Moiseienko M., Semerikov S. (2015). The mobile information and educational environment of higher educational institution. https://journal.iitta.gov.ua/index.php/itlt
title: Four core functions of an information and educational environment: informational, educational, controlling, organisational
description: The article enumerates the main functions of an information and educational environment: "інформаційна (задоволення інформаційно -освітніх потреб учасників навчального процесу)", "освітня (своєчасне та якісне забезпечення навчальним матеріалом)", a controlling function of supervising learners' independent work, and an organisational function of liaison with instructors. These functions frame what a mobile IEE must satisfy for all users.
requirements: An IEE must provide timely, quality learning materials and satisfy the informational-educational needs of all participants
constraints: The functions are stated for IEEs generally, not tested for mobile implementations specifically
key_sources: Moiseienko N., Moiseienko M., Semerikov S. (2015). The mobile information and educational environment of higher educational institution. https://journal.iitta.gov.ua/index.php/itlt

article_title: The mobile information and educational environment of higher educational institution
citation: Moiseienko N., Moiseienko M., Semerikov S. (2015). The mobile information and educational environment of higher educational institution. https://journal.iitta.gov.ua/index.php/itlt
title: IEE component groups divided by intended user type: general information, teaching-methodological materials, administrative information
description: The article divides the components of an information and educational environment into groups by intended user type: "Складові частини інформаційно-освітнього середовища можна умовно розділити на групи за типом користувачів". Group 1 is general information about the institution, educational services and student life; group 2 covers curricula, work programmes, methodological materials, e-library, specialised software, knowledge-assessment systems and instructor-student communication systems; group 3 is administrative documentation of departments and dean's offices.
requirements: Internet access through mobile learning devices is described as the leading way to reach these components at the current stage of ICT development
constraints: The grouping is presented as conditional (умовно) and descriptive, not empirically validated
examples: Group 2 includes forums and e-mail systems for teacher-student communication and an electronic library
key_sources: Moiseienko N., Moiseienko M., Semerikov S. (2015). The mobile information and educational environment of higher educational institution. https://journal.iitta.gov.ua/index.php/itlt

article_title: Designing Laboratories for Online Instruction using the iOLab Device
citation: Louis Leblond and Melissa Hicks. (2020). Designing Laboratories for Online Instruction using the iOLab Device. https://sites.psu.edu/lleblond/iolab/
title: iOLab handheld wireless lab device with multiple sensors and real-time data acquisition
description: The iOLab is a handheld, wheeled laboratory device developed by Mats Selen and Tim Stelzer at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, sold as of 2019 for $199 or rented from $42 for 3 months. It is "a handheld device on wheels equipped with a variety of sensors communicating wirelessly to a USB dongle", and its free software collects and presents data in real time with built-in statistical tools for slope and area under the curve. The authors used its wheel, force, accelerometer, gyro, magnetometer, analog input, barometer, sound and light sensors across mechanics and E&M labs, judging it cheaper and more versatile than third-party lab kits.
requirements: Students need the iOLab device, a computer with the free iOLab software, and for E&M the PASCO EM-8675 desktop electricity kit
constraints: The authors note students report "iOLab fatigue" if no other equipment is used throughout the semester; the PASCO smart cart has less friction but lacks the sensors needed for electricity and magnetism
target_learners: adult online learners in calculus-based introductory physics courses
examples: Mechanics labs listed in Table 1 include Exploration, Push and slide, Friction 1 and 2, Hooke's 1 and 2, and Rotation; E&M labs include Magnetic Field, Faraday's Law, and RC and RLC circuits
key_sources: Louis Leblond and Melissa Hicks. (2020). Designing Laboratories for Online Instruction using the iOLab Device. https://sites.psu.edu/lleblond/iolab/

article_title: Designing Laboratories for Online Instruction using the iOLab Device
citation: Louis Leblond and Melissa Hicks. (2020). Designing Laboratories for Online Instruction using the iOLab Device. https://sites.psu.edu/lleblond/iolab/
title: Three-phase weekly online lab unit: exploration, problem-solving, and revision with discussion board and peer review
description: Each weekly unit of the online course is structured in three phases: "exploration, problem solving, and revision". In the exploratory phase students read the textbook with web-based notes, videos, and interactive questions and post an initial discussion-board post; in the problem-solving phase the main interactions occur via a graded discussion board and a peer-review system in which students reply to teammates with questions, comments, compliments and/or connections and give feedback to two other students; teaching assistant and instructor feedback is provided throughout the week. Students submit a first draft individually, then a final lab report with a metacognitive reflection at the end of the unit.
requirements: Multiple assignments due throughout the week; discussion-board posts and peer feedback are required; TA and instructor feedback time of about 2 hours per week comparable to student lab time
constraints: Labs are shorter in length than in residential instruction partly because students work mostly individually and receive asynchronous feedback
target_learners: adult online learners, many working full time or with young children at home
examples: Students must submit a first discussion post by the end of the exploratory phase, are assigned peer-reviewers, and submit the final lab with a metacognitive reflection at week's end
key_sources: Louis Leblond and Melissa Hicks. (2020). Designing Laboratories for Online Instruction using the iOLab Device. https://sites.psu.edu/lleblond/iolab/

article_title: Education 5.0: Requirements, Enabling Technologies, and Future Directions
citation: Shabir Ahmad, Sabina Umirzakova, Ghulam Mujtaba, Muhammad Sadiq Amin, and Taegkeun Whangbo. (2023). Education 5.0: Requirements, Enabling Technologies, and Future Directions. https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.15846
title: IoT devices (wearables, sensors, smart devices) for personalized, collaborative, and remote learning
description: The article presents Internet of Things devices—"wearables, sensors, and smart devices"—as tools that collect real-time data on student learning and behavior to provide "a deeper understanding of individual student needs and abilities". IoT enables adaptive learning systems that adjust pace and content based on performance, personalized feedback (e.g., wearables tracking posture and movement), smart content such as connected textbooks, smart classrooms with smartboards and connected tablets, and remote collaboration through smartphones, tablets, and laptops.
requirements: Connectivity infrastructure so devices can share data and enable remote access
constraints: The element is described as a potential enabler within the Education 5.0 vision, not evaluated empirically in this article
target_learners: students in connected classrooms and remote learning settings
examples: Smart classrooms are described in which smartboards display and share information and students use connected tablets to participate in interactive activities and quizzes
key_sources: Shabir Ahmad, Sabina Umirzakova, Ghulam Mujtaba, Muhammad Sadiq Amin, and Taegkeun Whangbo. (2023). Education 5.0: Requirements, Enabling Technologies, and Future Directions. https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.15846
